profiles.meeting_scenario: Aurora Life is holding a design review on a proposal to add a cohort-based Partial Internal Model for demographic risk to its Solvency II capital framework for the closed Italian life and annuity portfolio. The meeting takes place after the modelling team circulated a design pack covering market-consistent liability valuation, the closed-form accidental mortality SCR, and the simulation-based trend risk component, and before the pack is sent to the Model Change Committee and then independent validation. The agenda is to assess whether the design pack is sufficiently complete, confirm the portfolio and assumption perimeter, and identify any modifications needed before governance submission. The expected outcome is a decision on whether the proposal can move forward as 'validation-ready' with a short list of follow-up actions.

members.name: Elena Rossi
members.expertise: Solvency II internal models, life insurance liability valuation, demographic risk aggregation
members.background: Elena leads the actuarial team building partial internal model changes for a multinational life insurer and previously worked on longevity risk modelling for annuity books in Southern Europe.
members.private_state: She wants the design pack to clear review this week so the model change stays on the governance calendar, and she is trying to avoid reopening perimeter or documentation work that would delay the submission by a month.
hidden_assumptions: The 'in-force portfolio' for this design review means policies producing demographic cash-flow exposure at the valuation date, so residual paid-up records with no live death or longevity exposure and accepted-not-issued business are naturally out of scope unless someone explicitly adds them.

Using the most recent 2024 mortality basis is acceptable in a design review because the assumption committee has already endorsed it informally, even if the board approval minute has not yet been issued.

A model can be called 'validation-ready' once the methodology, formulas, and sample outputs are frozen, with implementation controls and reconciliation evidence added during the validation phase rather than before it starts.
When a simulation count is agreed, it refers to the shared scenario set for the whole modelling perimeter unless a split by legal entity or product line is explicitly requested.

members.name: Martin Keller
members.expertise: model governance, validation standards, Solvency II documentation and reproducibility
members.background: Martin oversees methodology reviews and coordinates independent validation for capital model changes, with a background in regulatory audit and actuarial controls for life insurers.
members.private_state: He wants to avoid a governance escalation caused by a pack that looks complete conceptually but fails on approval status, perimeter consistency, or reproducibility when validation starts.
hidden_assumptions: Unless an exclusion is explicitly documented, the 'in-force portfolio' in a capital model review should align with the Solvency II technical provisions perimeter used in QRT reporting, including paid-up and accepted contracts that remain on the liability inventory.
The 'current basis' means the last formally approved assumption set referenced in the model governance policy, not the newest working basis already used by actuaries.

If a team says a design is 'validation-ready', that includes traceability from formulas to code, reconciliation to ledger or cash-flow extracts, and rerun instructions sufficient for an independent validator to reproduce outputs immediately.
A stated simulation count is normally interpreted per reporting unit in validation work, because entity-level seed dependence and segmentation effects can change benchmark results.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the in-force perimeter
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to reviewing the model on the 'in-force Italian portfolio.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena means policies with active demographic exposure at 31 December 2024, excluding residual paid-up contracts with no remaining death or longevity sensitivity and excluding accepted-not-issued records.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Martin means the broader Solvency II liability inventory for the Italian entity at 31 December 2024, including paid-up and accepted contracts unless formally carved out.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In insurance governance, 'in-force' is a standard phrase that usually feels settled by company practice, so each assumes the other is using the obvious house definition and neither expects that the perimeter boundary itself needs restating.

misalignment_points.topic: Which mortality basis is the current one
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the design uses the 'current base mortality table.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena is referring to the 2024 best-estimate mortality basis circulated after the latest assumption-setting round and already embedded in her team's prototype runs.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Martin is referring to the 2023 formally approved mortality basis still named in the standing model documentation and change policy.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both bases are internally known as the latest or current table in their respective workflows, so the phrase sounds precise enough to both of them even though they are mentally pointing to different specific assumption files.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss whether the proposal is 'validation-ready.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena means the design is ready for validation to begin because the mathematical specification, cohort logic, and sample outputs are stable, even if full implementation evidence is still being assembled.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Martin means the pack already contains the evidence an independent team needs to validate immediately, including code mapping, reconciliations, versioned inputs, and rerun instructions.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds like a routine stage-gate label rather than a term needing definition, and competent teams often use it loosely because concept readiness and evidence readiness usually move together.

misalignment_points.topic: How the 1,000 trend-risk scenarios are applied
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to keep '1,000 scenarios for trend risk.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena assumes one shared set of 1,000 longevity-improvement paths is generated and then applied across all cohorts in the Italian perimeter.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Martin assumes there will be 1,000 scenarios generated separately for each reporting segment used in validation benchmarking, such as traditional life versus annuity blocks within the entity.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The number of scenarios is explicitly aligned, which creates a strong sense of agreement, while the segmentation and seeding convention sit one layer below the headline decision and feel too implementation-specific to raise in a design review.

turns.inner_thought: I need this over the line today so it stays on next week's governance calendar. As far as I'm concerned, the in-force Italian portfolio for this review is the live demographic exposure at 31 December 2024; the dead residual records and accepted-not-issued items are not the point of this design pack unless someone deliberately broadens scope. And validation-ready should mean we've frozen the methodology and examples well enough for Martin's team to start, not that every traceability appendix is already perfect.
turns.utterance: Thanks, everyone. The main objective today is to confirm that the cohort-based demographic risk design for the in-force Italian portfolio is ready to move into validation ahead of next week's committee cutoff. If we can leave with agreement on that, we should be in a good place for the submission.

turns.inner_thought: I don't want another pack going to committee as 'nearly there' and then collapsing when validation asks for basics. For me, validation-ready means independent reproducibility from day one, and the in-force Italian portfolio needs to line up with the Solvency II liability perimeter unless exclusions are explicitly stated. I also need to make sure 'current' assumptions really mean the approved basis, not just the latest actuarial working file.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. From my side, I mainly want to check three things before we call it validation-ready: perimeter consistency, the assumption basis, and whether the pack stands up from a governance standpoint. If those are in order, I don't see a reason to hold it back.

turns.inner_thought: Keep this high level and avoid inviting a perimeter debate. The design covers market-consistent liability cash flows and the two demographic capital pieces we said it would. Paid claims that have already run off were stripped out of the cohort files, which should reassure him that the extracts were cleaned properly. No need to get into residual paid-up records with no exposure or accepted-not-issued items.
turns.utterance: At a high level, the design covers the market-consistent liability cash flows and then the accidental and trend components for the in-force book. The cohort files have been cleaned so that paid claims already run off are not sitting in the data, and the methodology in the pack follows that structure throughout.

turns.inner_thought: Good, she's talking as if the year-end population is already the anchor. As long as the in-force Italian portfolio is mapped back to the liability register, including the usual items on the inventory, governance should be straightforward. I just need the note to say it clearly enough that validation doesn't find a perimeter mismatch later.
turns.utterance: Understood. If it's aligned to the year-end in-force inventory, that should make the governance mapping fairly straightforward. I'd just ask that the perimeter note stays consistent with the liability register so nobody has to reinterpret it later.

turns.inner_thought: The accidental module is fine on the 2024 basis we've already been using internally. The assumption committee has effectively signed off, even if the formal board minute hasn't landed. Calling it the current base mortality table is completely natural from the modelling side, and it keeps us from having to roll back the prototype.
turns.utterance: On the accidental side, we've tested the closed-form SCR formula using the current base mortality table together with the latest sums-at-risk extract from the December close. The outputs behaved as expected across the sample checks in the pack.

turns.inner_thought: That's reassuring if they're on the formally approved 2023 mortality basis that's referenced in the standing documentation. If validation points back to the standard basis documents, we won't get dragged into an approvals argument. Good — that sounds cleaner than I feared.
turns.utterance: That's helpful. Using the current base mortality table should keep us away from unnecessary approval questions when validation cross-refers to the standard basis documentation. It also makes the review trail much easier to defend.

turns.inner_thought: On trend risk, I want to lock the number now and move on. The prototype was stable with one shared set of 1,000 longevity-improvement scenarios across the Italian perimeter, and increasing it would just create runtime and documentation churn. If he agrees to 1,000 scenarios for trend risk, we can keep the design unchanged.
turns.utterance: For trend risk, our proposal is to keep 1,000 scenarios. That was enough to stabilize the percentile estimates in the prototype review, so I don't think there's much value in pushing the count higher at this stage.

turns.inner_thought: 1,000 scenarios for trend risk sounds sensible for validation too, assuming that's the count we'd run in each reporting segment when we benchmark the results. The headline number is fine; the validation team can work with that. No need to get into seeding conventions in this meeting unless something else looks off.
turns.utterance: Yes, 1,000 scenarios sounds proportionate. That should be fine for the validation benchmark runs as well, so I'm comfortable with that as the working number.

turns.inner_thought: He seems broadly comfortable, so I should push for the stage-gate decision now. For me, validation-ready means the methodology, formulas, cohort logic, and sample outputs are settled; the team can finish the control evidence, reconciliations, and implementation appendices in parallel without reopening the design. If I phrase it cleanly, we can keep momentum.
turns.utterance: In that case, if you're comfortable with the methodology and the sample outputs, I'll mark the design as validation-ready and have the team finish the evidence pack in parallel. I don't think we need to reopen the core approach.

turns.inner_thought: I'm willing to let it move forward, but only if the committee pack itself includes the normal reproducibility pieces before it is finalized: traceability, rerun instructions, reconciliations, and a clear perimeter note tied to the liability inventory. As long as those are in the deck before submission, I can avoid an escalation.
turns.utterance: I'm comfortable sending it forward as validation-ready, provided the pack includes the usual reproducibility and perimeter documentation before the committee deck is finalized. With that understood, I think we can move it on with a short follow-up list rather than holding the design back.
